newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: European banks extend dominance in lending - BIS.
newsitem.headline: European banks extend dominance in lending - BIS.

text.p: Lending from industrial nations to developing countries surged by an unprecedented $60.7 billion or 6.59 percent in the first half of 1996 as European banks extended their dominance of international bank lending, the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) said on Sunday.
Also noteworthy was the fact that industrial companies in emerging nations increasingly borrowed directly from major international banks, bypassing their domestic banking systems, BIS said.

Lending from banks in industrial nations to developing nations rose $60.7 billion to $920.6 billion by mid-1996, with flows to Asia hitting a new record while lending to Eastern Europe and Latin America was sustained, BIS said in its latest survey of international bank lending.

The surge in lending was encouraged by improved economic management in borrowing countries, as well as the low level of interest rates and weak corporate demand in industrial countries which made major banks look elsewhere for high returns.

European banks aggressively expanded their involvement in the developing world and boosted their market share of all international lending to 54 percent compared with 14.2 percent for North American banks and 18.2 percent for Japanese banks.

BIS, central bank to the worlds' central banks, said business by North American banks showed signs of recovery, including a further return to Eastern and Central European markets after an almost complete retrenchment up to 1992.
In contrast, the extension of new credits by Japanese banks to developing nations came to a vitual standstill.
While European banks have been the most active in Latin America in the last decade, they also extended their lead over Japanese banks in the Asian region in the first half of 1996.
European banks -- especially German, French, Dutch and British -- raised their market share of lending to Asia to 40 percent by mid-1996 from 36 percent at the end of 1994.
Meanwhile, Japanese banks' share of Asian lending fell to 34 percent from 39 percent, while the share held by North American banks moved up to 11 percent from nine percent.

"This increased presence in Asia can be related not only to the liberalisation of local financial markets and the dynamism of the region, but also to the limited scope for expansion within Western Europe and the perceived difficulties in trying to access the U.S. market," BIS said.

The pace of new lending to Asia accelerated in the first half to a record $34.7 billion, with South Korea and Thailand accounting for more than half the total, followed at some distance by Indonesia, Malaysia, China and the Philippines.
The bulk of new funds in Asia was once again channelled to the non-bank private sector with its share of lending amounting to 48 percent of the total outstanding.

The reduced role of local banks partially reflects measures by some countries, for example Thailand and Korea, to restrict bank borrowing, or to liberalise capital outflows to reduce growing dependence on short-term funds and possible economic imbalances, such as overheating or a widening current account deficit.
Problems in a number of domestic banks and the privatisation of state enterprises were also factors behind the increased international borrowing by the non-bank sector, BIS said.
Worldwide, the non-bank sector now accounts for a record 42 percent of outstanding loans, up from 38 percent at end-1994.
While most of Europe's banks increased lending to Latin America, BIS noted Spanish banks ranked first in new lending.
BIS figures show that 13 percent of all international outstanding loans by Spanish banks to non-industrialised countries are to Mexican borrowers, well above 6.9 percent by British and French banks.

However, Spanish banks have a lot of catching up to do if they want to compete with U.S. and other European banks as the largest lenders to Mexico, which owes $57.1 billion to banks in industrialised countries that report to the BIS.

U.S. banks account for almost one-third of the outstanding loans, well-above French banks, the second largest group, which account for 11.3 percent. Spanish banks rank sixth with 5.2 percent of the outstanding claims on Mexico.
But Spanish banks are expanding in Latin America.
Spain's Banco Bilbao Vizcaya and Banco Santander have been on a buying spree throughout Latin America and are aggresively moving into retail banking in Mexico.
In December BBV purchased a 40 percent stake in Venezuela's largest bank Banco Provincial and Santander bought 90 percent stake in Banco de Venezuela, the country's second largest bank.
